entries.name: 5-wire
entries.hook: Long VGA and RGBHV cable runs for Resolume
entries.summary: An FFGL effect that puts a long run of VGA or RGBHV between the picture and the screen. Coax loses the square root of frequency, and that one fact gives the soft picture, the streak behind every caption and the displaced ghost — all from the same curve rather than three separate effects. The equaliser at the far end brings the picture back and lifts the noise with it; the identical filter at the amplifier does not.

entries.name: Amber
entries.summary: Resolume opens neither .swf nor .flv, so a decade and a half of VJ loops, web animation and motion tests sits in formats nothing on the machine will play. Amber is two halves: a converter that turns them into DXV or Hap with the frame rate and transparency intact, and an FFGL source plugin that plays Flash live on a layer with its timeline and ActionScript actually running. Powered by Ruffle. No audio — FFGL has no audio path.

About: name Stoatworks Labs in the plugin's own controls, and link the support page

First release. Two halves of the same problem: Resolume opens neither `.swf` nor `.flv`.

## The converter

`tools/amber` — Python, cross-platform, drives your own ffmpeg and your own build of Ruffle's exporter.

```bash
tools/amber doctor                          # what can this machine do?
tools/amber convert ~/clips -o ~/converted
```

- **`.flv`** — Sorenson Spark, VP6, VP6-with-alpha, H.264, Screen Video
- **`.swf`** — rendered through [Ruffle](https://ruffle.rs), muxed at the rate in the SWF header
- **Output**: DXV by default, **Hap Alpha whenever the source carries transparency**, Hap Q on request, ProRes 4444 as an alpha fallback

## The plugin

`Amber.bundle` / `Amber.dll` — an FFGL source that plays `.swf` live on a Resolume layer, timeline and ActionScript really running.

Parameters: Movie, Run, Restart, Speed, Scaling (Fit / Fill / Stretch), Smoothing, **Transparent** (on by default — Flash's own `wmode=transparent`, so it works as an overlay).

**Install:** drop `Amber.bundle` into `~/Library/Graphics/FreeFrame Plug-Ins`, or `Amber.dll` into your Resolume FFGL folder, and restart Resolume.

## Two ffmpeg behaviours worth knowing

Both were found by measurement, both are silent, and both will bite anything else built on DXV:

- **DXV corrupts any width that is not a multiple of 16.** It reports success, records the right dimensions, and writes a diagonally sheared picture. **550×400 is the default Flash stage size**, so a naive pipeline mangles a large share of all Flash ever made. amber aligns around it, and re-measures the rule on every test run.
- **DXV cannot carry alpha** — one format, `dxt1`, self-described "No Alpha" — and flattens it without warning. Alpha content is routed to Hap Alpha instead, which was measured byte-exact.

Also measured: plain `hap` is *identical* in quality to DXV (both DXT1) but 27% larger, so it is never the better choice. `hap_q` is +1.8 dB with the worst-case error halved, for ~80% more size.

## What it can't do

- **No audio, anywhere.** FFGL provides no audio path at all, so live Flash is silent whatever it contains, and the converter drops audio for the same reason.
- **Ruffle runs inside Resolume's process.** Every call is guarded, which turns most bad content into a black layer rather than a crash — but a guard is not a process boundary, and content that hard-crashes Ruffle takes Resolume with it. There is no out-of-process helper yet.
- **Live playback is `.swf` only.** `.flv` goes through the converter.
- **The converter cannot produce transparent output from `.swf`.** It drives Ruffle's `exporter` binary, which has no background option. The plugin can.
- **No seek or scrub parameter** on the plugin.

## What has and hasn't been verified

**Verified:** the plugin confirmed working in Resolume Arena on Apple Silicon. The converter against real content — real 2003-era Flash, and real-world FLV in Sorenson Spark (720p and 4K) and VP6 — with output re-decoded and compared to source pixels each time. VP6-with-alpha verified using a test file assembled from existing VP6 bitstreams (ffmpeg decodes VP6 but cannot encode it); alpha survives at a mean error of 0.05. 45 tests, plus a GL harness and a real FFGL host.

**Not verified:** only the Apple Silicon slice has been run in a host — neither the Intel half of the universal bundle nor the Windows build has been loaded into a Resolume. Check it in your own rig before a show depends on it.

Full detail, including every trap found along the way, is in [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/amber/blob/main/AGENTS.md).

entries.name: Aquilon VPU Map
entries.hook: Where every mixer in the chassis went
entries.summary: Every layer on an Analog Way LivePremier costs physical mixing hardware, and the frame knows exactly where that hardware went. This reads the allocation back and draws the whole chassis on one screen — each VPU as the 8x8 field of links the manual draws it as, every layer's bar as wide as the outputs it spans and as tall as its capacity. It reads and never writes.
entries.blurb: Every layer costs physical mixing hardware, and a frame will not tell you a configuration does not fit until it fails to fit. This reads the allocation back and draws the whole chassis on one screen, each VPU as the 8x8 field of links the manual draws it as. It also diffs the running map against the staged one, which catches the case where every difference is a link moving and no property changes at all.
entries.role: Where every mixer in the chassis went

entries.name: Asciify
entries.summary: An ASCII art FFGL effect that matches each character cell on how much ink it wants and on where that ink sits, so edges pick up characters that lean the right way instead of being flattened into a brightness ramp.
entries.blurb: A character renderer rather than a brightness ramp. A cell is a small picture, and the glyph that stands in for it is the one whose ink is distributed most like it — how much ink there is and where it sits, measured on the same grid for the cell and for every character in the set.

lines:
### Background Opacity is now Background Alpha

The control that sets how opaque the plugin's own background is was declared as
`Background Opacity` — 18 characters. FFGL hands the host a **16-character**
name buffer, so Resolume has been drawing it cut off, as **Background Opaci**.
It is now **Background Alpha**, which is exactly 16 and displays in full.

It is the same control, doing the same thing, with the same range and default.
Only the name changed. If you address it by name — an OSC path, a MIDI or
shortcut mapping, a preset made by another tool — re-check that mapping. The
OpenFX build's label changed with it, so the control reads the same in Resolume
and in Resolve; the id the two hosts persist is unchanged, so existing projects
keep their values.

### A User guide button in the About block

About now carries four buttons instead of three: **User guide**, Project page,
Source on GitHub, Support the work. The guide button is new, and opens the
published guide for this plugin.

### The OpenFX plugin now ships for Linux

There is a `-ofx-linux-x86_64` build in this release, for Resolve on Linux. It
is checked by loading it in a Rocky 8 container — the oldest glibc Resolve
supports — and calling the two entry points a host calls first, rather than
inferring from the build that it would load.

---

Full changelog: https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/burin/compare/v0.1.3...v0.1.4

## Speed and timing changes no longer move the picture

Moving **Rate** made the zoom and the drift both teleport. The drawing now stays where it is and changes pace.

**Why it happened.** The position was computed as `clock × Rate`, so changing
Rate moved it by `clock × the change` — and `clock` is however long the
composition has been open. Ten minutes in, a small nudge is worth tens of
cycles; an hour in, hundreds. It looked like the animation restarting from a
specific position, which is exactly how it was reported.

**What changes now.** The position reached so far is carried forward and
counting continues from there at the new rate. Rate changes the pace and nothing
else, which is what it should always have done.

**What deliberately still jumps.** Beat and Bar sync re-lock to the host's
transport — landing a cycle on the bar line is the whole point of them, and
smoothing that would slide the animation off the grid. The OpenFX build (Resolve,
Nuke, Natron, Vegas) keeps the plain calculation too, because a timeline host
renders arbitrary frames in arbitrary order and can keyframe Rate.

Nothing else about the output changes. A composition saved with an earlier
version opens looking exactly the same.

Reported by an external user against Orrery, as
[orrery#6](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/6); the same
arithmetic was in most of the plugin fleet and is being fixed across all of it.

entries.name: Cartridge
entries.hook: A console emulator as a live Resolume source
entries.summary: A libretro frontend that runs inside Resolume as an FFGL generator: point it at a core and a game and the console becomes a layer, with the joypad MIDI-mapped onto whatever controller is already on the desk. Ships as two builds — in-process, and an out-of-process helper that keeps the show up when a core crashes. No cores, BIOS images or games are included.
entries.blurb: A libretro frontend as a source layer: point it at an emulator core and a game and the console becomes a layer you can composite, key and run through everything else in the rig — with the joypad MIDI-mapped onto whatever controller is already on the desk. It was built as a companion to Old Cathode, because a 240p frame through a real composite encoder is the thing it exists to make possible.

testrom: a GBA test card you build yourself
docs: point at the test card from where people look for content
About: name Stoatworks Labs in the plugin's own controls, and link the support page

A [libretro](https://www.libretro.com/) frontend that runs inside Resolume Arena
and Avenue as an FFGL generator. Point it at a core and a game and the console
becomes a layer — composite it, key it, run it through other effects, and
MIDI-map the joypad onto whatever controller is already on the desk.

Built as a companion to [old-cathode](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/old-cathode):
a 240p Mega Drive frame through a real composite encoder, with dot crawl and
cross-colour that are consequences rather than decoration, is the thing this
exists to make possible.

## Two builds, one frontend

|  | **In process** (the plugin) | **Out of process** (the helper) |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Same frame it was produced | One composition frame later |
| A core crashes | **Resolume goes down with it** | The helper dies, the show continues |
| Two of one core | Needs a private-copy workaround | Free — separate processes |

Rehearsal and studio work: in process. Anything with an audience: the helper.

## No cores, no BIOS, no games

None are included and none ever will be. You supply your own, exactly as with
RetroArch. **[docs/CORES.md](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/cartridge/blob/main/docs/CORES.md)**
is how to get them — which core for which console, and the two macOS traps
(architecture matching and Gatekeeper quarantine) that otherwise cost an
afternoon. Cores are `dlopen`ed at runtime and never redistributed, so their
licence terms are between you and their authors.

## What has been verified — and what has not

`tools/verify.sh` passes end to end against a **synthetic libretro core built
into the repo**: the CPU host (pixel formats, padded pitch, triple buffer, input
ports, audio ring, determinism, two instances staying separate), the real plugin
class through the real FFGL sequence in a headless GL 4.1 core context at two
aspects, a real second process, and the helper killed with `SIGKILL` underneath
a running consumer.

**It has not been loaded into Resolume, and has not been run against a real
emulator core.** How the parameter groups land in Resolume's inspector, and
whether a controller MIDI-maps onto the pad, are unconfirmed. Check it in your
own rig before a show depends on it.

## Install

macOS universal (Apple Silicon and Intel). Drop `Cartridge.bundle` into
Resolume's Extra Effects folder, restart, and it appears alongside the built-in
sources. For the out-of-process path, run `cartridge-helper` first.

The build is unsigned, so macOS warns once before it will load it.

The source carries Windows and Linux branches; **neither has been built or
tested**, and there is no binary for either here.

entries.name: Flenser
entries.hook: A liquid light show, for Resolume
entries.summary: Oil, water, alcohol and dye between two watch glasses on an overhead projector — the 1967 liquid light show, as an FFGL source and a matching effect that puts your clip where the lamp was. The cells are dye filters, so where they cross they multiply rather than add.
entries.blurb: A liquid light show: oil, water, alcohol and dye between two watch glasses on an overhead projector. Ships as two plugins — a source that is the wheel with its own lamp behind it, and an effect that puts your clip where the lamp was, so the footage is what shines through the oil.

lines:
The first release. Oil, water, alcohol and dye between two watch glasses on an overhead projector, as **four plugins from one model**: an FFGL source and effect for Resolume Arena/Avenue, and an OpenFX generator and filter for DaVinci Resolve, Nuke, Natron and Vegas — on macOS, Windows and Linux.

**The colour is subtractive.** Every cell is a dye filter, so where two cross they *multiply*: cyan over magenta is blue, not white, and all three inks together are nearly black. That is the difference between a dyed wheel and every blob effect that adds its colours.

**Every cell's edge is a lens.** The meniscus displaces what is behind it, splits it by wavelength, and throws a bright caustic just inside a dark rim — an edge band, because the middle of a cell is flat oil between two flat glasses and bends almost nothing.

**Flenser Lamp puts your clip where the projector's lamp was**, so the footage is what shines through the oil. Three modes: project through it, lay the lit oil over it, or take only its brightness and let the dye supply the colour.

Eight factory presets, shared by all four plugins from one table — Overhead Projector, Optikinetics, Alcohol Burn, Ink in Water, Sodium, Clear Water, Beading, Slow Bloom.

### What is verified

Everything is a pure function of position and time, which is what makes the model checkable at all:

- the GLSL half and the C++ half agree across **1,625,010 values** over every control, with nothing past 5e-4
- a clear wheel leaves a picture **byte-identical**: 0 of 230,400 bytes differ through the Resolume build, 0 of 921,600 through the OpenFX build
- all **33 controls** measurably reach the picture, in both bundles
- 8 presets × 3 host behaviours × 2 bundles
- the Linux OpenFX bundle is built for glibc 2.28 and proved to `dlopen` on Rocky 8, reporting both plugins

`Simmer` — a bounded feedback trail — is Resolume-only by design: an OpenFX host renders frames out of order and cannot match its own preview with a feedback buffer.

### What is not

**It has not been loaded into Resolume, or into Resolve.** Everything above runs the plugin directly or through a probe host. No Windows build has been run, and the Linux load test is a load, not a render. Check it in your own rig before trusting it in a show.

Try it in a browser first, with nothing uploaded: <https://flenser-demo.stoatworks-labs.com>

entries.name: Flipbook
entries.hook: Play a sprite sheet in Resolume
entries.summary: A page of stills, cut into a grid and played as an animation — as an FFGL source and a matching effect for Resolume, and an OpenFX plugin for Resolve. Up to sixty-four copies with a stagger, so one animation travels through the field rather than sixty-four doing the same thing at once.
entries.blurb: A page of stills, cut into a grid and played as an animation — VFX sheets, game sprite rows, pixel art kept as pixel art, or an animated GIF that brings its own frame count. The effect can take the clip it sits on as the sheet, so Resolume's own media management does the file handling.

lines:
### Background Opacity is now Background Alpha

The control that sets how opaque the plugin's own background is was declared as
`Background Opacity` — 18 characters. FFGL hands the host a **16-character**
name buffer, so Resolume has been drawing it cut off, as **Background Opaci**.
It is now **Background Alpha**, which is exactly 16 and displays in full.

It is the same control, doing the same thing, with the same range and default.
Only the name changed. If you address it by name — an OSC path, a MIDI or
shortcut mapping, a preset made by another tool — re-check that mapping. The
OpenFX build's label changed with it, so the control reads the same in Resolume
and in Resolve; the id the two hosts persist is unchanged, so existing projects
keep their values.

### A User guide button in the About block

About now carries four buttons instead of three: **User guide**, Project page,
Source on GitHub, Support the work. The guide button is new, and opens the
published guide for this plugin.

### The OpenFX plugin now ships for Linux

There is a `-ofx-linux-x86_64` build in this release, for Resolve on Linux. It
is checked by loading it in a Rocky 8 container — the oldest glibc Resolve
supports — and calling the two entry points a host calls first, rather than
inferring from the build that it would load.

---

Full changelog: https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/flipbook/compare/v1.0.3...v1.0.4

## Speed and timing changes no longer move the picture

Moving **Rate** cut the sheet to an unrelated cell. Playback now continues from the cell on screen at the new rate.

**Why it happened.** The position was computed as `clock × Rate`, so changing
Rate moved it by `clock × the change` — and `clock` is however long the
composition has been open. Ten minutes in, a small nudge is worth tens of
cycles; an hour in, hundreds. It looked like the animation restarting from a
specific position, which is exactly how it was reported.

**What changes now.** The position reached so far is carried forward and
counting continues from there at the new rate. Rate changes the pace and nothing
else, which is what it should always have done.

**What deliberately still jumps.** Beat and Bar sync re-lock to the host's
transport — landing a cycle on the bar line is the whole point of them, and
smoothing that would slide the animation off the grid. The OpenFX build (Resolve,
Nuke, Natron, Vegas) keeps the plain calculation too, because a timeline host
renders arbitrary frames in arbitrary order and can keyframe Rate.

Nothing else about the output changes. A composition saved with an earlier
version opens looking exactly the same.

Reported by an external user against Orrery, as
[orrery#6](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/6); the same
arithmetic was in most of the plugin fleet and is being fixed across all of it.

[orrery#6](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/6); the same
arithmetic was in most of the plugin fleet and is being fixed across all of it.

**3D Maze now walks the maze, instead of pacing the same few cells.**

The walk turned round at a dead end and then preferred to carry straight on at every junction on the way back — which, travelling backwards, is exactly the corridor it had arrived down. So it retraced its approach, hit the dead end at the far end of it, and did the whole thing again. On the factory 3D Maze preset the camera saw fifty of a hundred cells in twelve minutes of playback, and spent a full minute inside nine of them.

It now counts how often it has left each cell along each heading and chooses among the least-used ways out, so a corridor it has already been down loses to one it has not. **Density** keeps its job — deciding between exits that are equally unexplored — and still gives long corridors when set low.

Nothing else changed: same eleven savers, same controls, same presets. The browser demo at [idler-demo.stoatworks-labs.com](https://idler-demo.stoatworks-labs.com) carries the same fix.

lines:
## Glitch Rate no longer re-rolls the machine's luck

Moving **Glitch Rate** made every corruption event re-roll at once, so the
picture convulsed the instant the control was touched instead of simply
glitching faster or slower.

**Why it happened.** The glitch tick was computed as `clock × rate`, so changing
the rate skipped the tick forward by `clock × the change` — thousands of ticks,
an hour into a composition.

**What changes now.** The tick count reached so far is carried forward and
counting continues from there at the new rate.

**One deliberate improvement.** Winding Glitch Rate down to **0** now holds the
glitch that is on screen at that moment, rather than snapping back to the very
first one. You can ride the control down onto a frame you like and freeze it —
which is what the still was always meant to be for. Loading a composition that
has never had the control touched still starts in exactly the same place as
before, so nothing you have saved will open differently.

Same root cause as [orrery#6](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/6),
reported by an external user; it is being fixed across the plugin fleet.

entries.name: nib
entries.summary: An FFGL effect that turns a clip into ink — continuous, closed strokes on paper rather than a glowing outline. Most edge effects ask how fast tone is changing at each pixel, which gives a magnitude with no memory of direction. nib works out which way the drawing runs first, then steers a difference of Gaussians across the flow and a line integral convolution along it, so a pixel whose neighbours agree survives and one that fired on its own does not.
entries.blurb: Line drawing rather than edge glow: continuous, closed strokes in ink on paper. It works out which way the drawing runs before it filters, then runs a band-pass across the flow and a smoothing along it — so a pixel whose neighbours agree survives, and one that fired on its own does not. Eight instruments, from Pen and Ink to Cyanotype and Woodcut.

entries.name: Old Cathode
entries.hook: Analogue TV signal path for Resolume
entries.summary: An FFGL effect that models the route a picture took to reach a television, rather than the look of one. Universal macOS bundle and Windows DLL.
entries.blurb: An analogue television signal path rather than the look of one. It encodes the picture onto a colour subcarrier the way a broadcast encoder would have, damages the composite waveform as a single signal, and decodes it again with no more information than a real receiver had — then paints the result onto a phosphor screen behind curved glass.

lines:
## Vertical Hold no longer teleports the raster

Moving **Vertical Hold** made the picture jump to an unrelated vertical offset
instead of starting to roll. It now rolls from where the picture is.

**Why it happened.** The roll was computed as `Vertical Hold × clock`, so
changing the control moved the roll by `clock × the change` — and `clock` is
however long the composition has been open. Because the roll wraps, the result
was not a faster roll but a picture that landed somewhere arbitrary: the raster
teleporting rather than the hold slipping, which is a worse fault than the one
the control exists to imitate.

**What changes now.** The walk reached so far is carried forward and continues
from there at the new rate. Riding Vertical Hold up from zero now does what it
looks like it should — the picture starts to crawl, then run.

**What is unchanged.** The rolling bar's width still follows the control
directly, the OpenFX build (Resolve, Nuke, Natron, Vegas) keeps the plain
calculation because a timeline host renders arbitrary frames in arbitrary order,
and nothing else about the output moves. A composition saved with an earlier
version opens looking exactly the same.

Same root cause as [orrery#6](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/6),
reported by an external user; it is being fixed across the plugin fleet.

About: name Stoatworks Labs in the plugin's own controls, and link the support page

Two things, both from [#6](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/6) and [#7](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/issues/7).

## Speed no longer teleports the shapes

Changing **Speed** used to jump every instance to a new position, as though the animation had restarted. The phase was `clock × speed`, and the clock is however long the composition has been open — so an hour in, a small nudge to the slider is worth hundreds of cycles.

The phase reached so far is now carried forward and counting starts again from there at the new rate: the shapes stay where they are and simply change pace. **Free** sync only — **Beat** and **Bar** still re-lock to the transport on purpose, because phase 0 landing on the bar line is what those modes are for.

The host clock work behind the v1.0.0 fix has also been tightened. Instead of guessing the unit from a single frame delta, it measures the host's clock against a real one over several frames, fails safe to the wall clock while undecided, and says in the log which unit it settled on.

## Shade

New **Shade** and **Light** controls light a shape as though it had been inflated. The normal comes out of the same distance field that draws the shape, so on a **Circle** it is exactly a sphere; every other primitive rounds the way its own field says it should, which makes a **Star** faceted along its spines and a **Triangle** barely domed at all.

Off by default. A shape with `Shade` at zero renders exactly as it did before.

## Also

`CMakeLists.txt` had been left at 1.0.0, so v1.0.1's bundles reported the wrong version inside correctly named files. Fixed.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/orrery/compare/v1.0.1...v1.0.2

entries.hook: See your lighting programming, before the room
entries.summary: A lightweight lighting visualiser. Drop in an MVR and it reads the rig straight out of it — fixture positions, patch, and the GDTF definitions embedded alongside, so it knows which channel is pan, how wide the beam opens and whether the colour mixes additively or subtractively. Then feed it Art-Net, sACN or DMX off a USB interface and watch the programming in volumetric haze, from anywhere you care to put the camera. Pixel-mapped fixtures work properly: a wall that declares four template channels across a hundred references is resolved to the three hundred it actually occupies, one DMX slot per pixel. The desktop build takes the live input; the hosted build imports and flies the same rig in a browser tab with a built-in demo look, because Art-Net and sACN are UDP and a browser cannot receive it.

entries.name: SRT Router
entries.summary: A broadcast-router-style crosspoint for SRT: any number of inputs and outputs, each output live-switchable to one source, added and removed at runtime from a web UI. Pure relay, no transcode. NDI transport included.

entries.summary: Injects out-of-tree kernel modules into a SquashFS initrd and writes it to bootable removable media. You supply the image and the modules — useful when an installer doesn't know about your NIC or RAID card.

entries.name: Tinsel
entries.summary: An FFGL effect that finds the outlines in a clip and lights them like a string of LEDs, running the patterns an LED controller runs — chases, comets, twinkles, fire — over twenty patterns and sixteen palettes.
entries.blurb: Finds the outlines in whatever is on the layer, hangs a string of virtual lamps along them, and runs the sort of pattern an LED controller runs — chases, comets, twinkles, fire, a scanner, a wipe. Point it at a logo and it becomes a neon sign, a theatre marquee or a Christmas tree.

lines: About: name Stoatworks Labs in the plugin's own controls, and link the support page

First stable release.

## Alphabetised dropdowns — and your compositions are safe

The **Pattern** and **Palette** dropdowns are now in alphabetical order instead of the order the enum happened to be written in ([#4](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/issues/4)).

**Nothing to re-pick after updating.** FFGL stores the *value* behind a dropdown entry rather than its position, and `SetParamElementInfo` takes the display slot and the stored value separately — so the lists are sorted for you while every entry keeps the number it shipped with. Twinkle is still 11; it has just moved down the list. Existing compositions, clips and presets point at exactly the same pattern and palette they always did.

Three lists deliberately keep their order, because there the position *is* the meaning: **Sync** (Free → Beat → Bar is a progression), **Preset** (Custom is pinned at the top — it isn't a preset, it's the statement that you aren't on one), and the two colour-picker-driven entries at the head of **Palette**.

This applies to the **Resolume/FFGL** build only. OFX's `appendOption` has no way to separate the display slot from the stored value, so sorting there would repoint existing Resolve/Nuke/Natron projects. Both builds still map the same value to the same pattern.

## Also since v0.2.0

- **Factory presets** — eight pattern-and-palette pairings, driving both builds from one table.
- **BPM sync and an FFT audio input** — drive the animation from the host clock or from audio.
- **Host clock normalised** — measured live in Arena 7.27.1, `SetTime` arrives in milliseconds while the FFGL header specifies no unit. Read as seconds it froze the synced modes solid and made Free mode spin at the delta clamp. The unit is now decided from the first plausible frame delta, so both kinds of host run correctly.
- **macOS builds are signed and notarised by Apple** and open with no Gatekeeper warning. Windows builds remain unsigned, so SmartScreen warns once.
- **Browser demo** at [tinsel-demo.stoatworks-labs.com](https://tinsel-demo.stoatworks-labs.com), with an `?embed=1` mode for use as a video source.
- **CI** so pull requests get a status check, and `ATTRIBUTIONS.md`.

## What's Changed
* Build(deps): Bump actions/download-artifact from 4 to 8 by @dependabot[bot] in https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/pull/1
* Build(deps): Bump actions/checkout from 4 to 7 by @dependabot[bot] in https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/pull/2
* Build(deps): Bump actions/upload-artifact from 4 to 7 by @dependabot[bot] in https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/pull/3
* Add a CI workflow so pull requests get a status check by @stoatworks-labs in https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/pull/6

## New Contributors
* @dependabot[bot] made their first contribution in https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/pull/1
* @stoatworks-labs made their first contribution in https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/tinsel/pull/6

entries.name: Vertigo
entries.summary: An FFGL effect that performs the shot where the camera tracks backwards while the lens zooms in, so one surface stays exactly the size it was and everything at any other distance moves. It can invent the depth it needs, so it works on any clip — or read a real depth map out of the picture.
entries.blurb: The dolly zoom: the camera tracks along its own axis while the lens zooms the other way, so one surface stays exactly the size it was and everything at another distance moves. It can invent the depth it needs and work on any clip, or read a real depth map out of the picture.

lines: About: name Stoatworks Labs in the plugin's own controls, and link the support page

## Factory presets work

Reported in [#2](https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/vertigo/issues/2): choosing any preset did nothing and the dropdown snapped straight back to **Custom**.

Resolume does not act on the value events a plugin raises when it changes its own parameters. It keeps pushing the values it still believes in — the ones from before the preset — and those arrive looking exactly like an operator moving a slider, which is what the plugin took them for. So the preset was being applied and then immediately abandoned, every time.

A preset is now an override rather than a write: the render and the parameter read-back both take the preset's value for anything it covers, and the plugin tracks what the host last *sent* separately so it can tell an operator's edit from the host restating itself. Moving a covered slider still drops to **Custom**, as it should.

Dropping to Custom is now logged with the values that caused it, so the next report of anything like this is answerable from the log rather than from a code read.

## Also

`CMakeLists.txt` had been left at 0.1.0, so v0.1.1's bundle reported the wrong version inside a correctly named file. Fixed.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/stoatworks-labs/vertigo/compare/v0.1.1...v0.1.2

entries.name: WebLinked
entries.hook: A URL in, SDI, NDI and a screen out
entries.summary: Renders any web page offscreen through Chromium at a broadcast raster and rate, then sends it to DeckLink and AJA over SDI, to the network as NDI and OMT, and fullscreen to a GPU-attached display — every output taking the same frame. It can run several such pipelines at once, each with its own browser, clock and raster, so a page that hangs on one feed cannot touch the others. The engine clocks the browser one frame at a time rather than letting it paint on its own timer, so 50 ticks a second really is 50 paints. Settings, live diagnostics and an interactive preview are all in the browser, so a rack machine needs nothing but an HTTP port.

entries.name: WSM–WWB Bridge
entries.summary: Moves frequency-coordination data between Shure Wireless Workbench and Sennheiser Wireless Systems Manager. Reads and writes both native formats, reverse-engineered from real exports, plus a generic CSV column mapper.
entries.blurb: Moves coordination data between Shure Wireless Workbench and Sennheiser Wireless Systems Manager, reading and writing both native formats plus a generic CSV column mapper. A Python desktop tool — useful when a browser isn't the right shape.
